'''Sir Andre Konstantin Geim''' ({{langx|ru|Андре́й Константи́нович Гейм}}; born 21 October 1958) is a Russian-born British-Dutch [[physicist]]. Geim was appointed as a [[Chair (professorship)|chair professor]] at the [[University of Hong Kong]] and assumed his tenure in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chan |first=Anne |last2=Ihara |first2=Kensaku |title=Hong Kong woos global scholars as West tightens China scrutiny |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/spotlight/immigration/hong-kong-woos-global-scholars-as-west-tightens-china-scrutiny |access-date=2026-10-03 |website=Nikkei Asia |language=en}}</ref>

Geim was awarded the 2010 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] jointly with [[Konstantin Novoselov]] for his work on [[graphene]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Geim |first=A. K. |author-link=Andre Geim |year=2009 |title=Graphene: Status and Prospects |journal=Science |volume=324 |issue=5934 |pages=1530–1534 |arxiv=0906.3799 |bibcode=2009Sci...324.1530G |doi=10.1126/science.1158877 |pmid=19541989 |s2cid=206513254}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Geim |first1=A. K. |last2=Novoselov |first2=K. S. |year=2007 |title=The rise of graphene |journal=Nature Materials |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=183–191 |arxiv=cond-mat/0702595 |bibcode=2007NatMa...6..183G |doi=10.1038/nmat1849 |pmid=17330084 |s2cid=14647602}}</ref> At that time he was a [[Dutch citizen]].<ref name=citizen>{{Cite news |last=Livni |first=Ephrat |date=2025-07-04 |title=Nobel Prize-Winning Physicist Is Stripped of Dutch Citizenship |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/04/world/europe/nobel-physicist-dutch-citizenship-revoked.html |access-date=2025-07-04 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He later became a [[British citizen]] to accept a [[Knighthood (UK)|knighthood]] and considered himself [[Dutch people in the United Kingdom|Dutch-British]].<ref name="Volkskrant">{{Cite web |title=Nederlandse Nobelprijswinnaar is zijn nationaliteit kwijt. 'Ik ben het land uitgeschopt als een nutteloos ding' |trans-title=Dutch Nobel Prize winner has lost his nationality. ‘I was kicked out of the country like a useless thing’ |last=Klerck |first=Hanneke de |work=de Volkskrant |date=2025-07-02 |access-date=2025-07-02 |url= https://www.volkskrant.nl/buitenland/nederlandse-nobelprijswinnaar-is-zijn-nationaliteit-kwijt-ik-ben-het-land-uitgeschopt-als-een-nutteloos-ding~ba943b63/ |language=nl}}</ref> 

Previously he was working in England in the [[School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Manchester|School of Physics and Astronomy]] at the [[University of Manchester]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Andre Geim, FRS (Condensed Matter Physics Group – The University of Manchester) |url=http://www.condmat.physics.manchester.ac.uk/people/academic/geim/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120423112543/http://www.condmat.physics.manchester.ac.uk/people/academic/geim/ |archive-date=23 April 2012}}</ref><ref name="Volkskrant" /> Geim has been [[Regius Professor]] of Physics and [[Royal Society]] Research Professor at the [[National Graphene Institute]]. 

He was also previously awarded an [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in 2000 for levitating a frog using its intrinsic magnetism. He is the first and only individual, as of 2026, to have received both Nobel and Ig Nobel prizes, for which he holds a Guinness World Record.

==Education==
Andre Geim was born to Konstantin Alekseyevich Geim and Nina Nikolayevna Bayer in [[Sochi]], Russia, on 21 October 1958. Both his parents were engineers of German origin; Geim says his maternal great-grandmother was Jewish.<ref name="NobelBio">{{Cite web |title=Andre Geim – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2010/geim/biographical/ |access-date=8 May 2023 |website=nobelprize.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=RG-RB – 42 |url=http://www.rg-rb.de/2010/42/odi.shtml |access-date=30 October 2010 |publisher=Rg-rb.de }}{{Dead link|date=August 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> His grandfather Nikolay N. Bayer (Mykola Baier in Ukrainian) was a notable public figure in Ukraine of the early 20th century, one of its first nature conservationists and the founder/first rector of [[Kamyanets-Podilsky Ivan Ohienko National University|Kaminiets-Podilskyi University]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Baier |first1=Mykola |url=https://figshare.com/articles/Lets_respect_and_protect_our_native_land_/10271936 |title=Lets respect and protect our native land. |last2=Oleksii |first2=Vasyliuk |date=8 November 2019 |publisher=figshare |language=en |doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.10271936.v1}}</ref><ref>Wikipedia page in Ukrainian: [[:uk:Баєр Микола Миколайович|Баєр Микола Миколайович]]</ref>

In 1965, the family moved to [[Nalchik]],<ref name="GRHC">{{cite press release |url=http://library.ndsu.edu/grhc/outreach/friends/geim1.html |title=Andre Geim, a German Russian, is Awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics |work=Germans from Russia Heritage Collection |publisher=[[North Dakota State University]] |date=October 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727115816/http://library.ndsu.edu/grhc/outreach/friends/geim1.html |access-date=25 October 2010 |archive-date=2011-07-27 }}</ref> where he studied at a high school.<ref name=GRHC/> After graduation, he applied to the [[Moscow Engineering Physics Institute]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rusdeutsch.ru/?news=2332 |title=Знай наших: лауреатом Нобелевской премии по физике стал российский немец |trans-title=Know our people: a Russian German won the Nobel Prize in Physics |lang=ru |work=rusdeutsch.ru |date=6 October 2010 |access-date=27 October 2010 }}</ref> He took the entrance exams twice, but attributes his failure to qualify to discrimination on account of his German ethnicity.<ref name="NobelBio" /> He then applied to the [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]] (MIPT), where he was accepted.

He said that at the time he would not have chosen to study [[solid-state physics]], preferring particle physics or astrophysics, but is now happy with his choice.<ref name=Murphy/> He received a [[diplom]] ([[Master of Science|MSc]] degree equivalent) from MIPT in 1982 and a [[Candidate of Sciences]] (PhD equivalent) degree in [[metal physics]] in 1987 from the [[Institute of Solid State Physics (Russia)|Institute of Solid State Physics]] (ISSP) at the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] (RAS) in [[Chernogolovka]].<ref name="Murphy">{{cite news |last=Murphy |first=John |url=https://www.scientific-computing.com/feature/renaissance-scientist-fund-ideas?feature_id=1 |title=Renaissance scientist with fund of ideas |work=Scientific Computing World |date=15 July 2006 |access-date=27 October 2010 }}</ref><ref name="CV">{{DOClink|[http://onnes.ph.man.ac.uk/~geim/Geim%20CV&resume.doc Geim's CV]|56.5&nbsp;KB}}. [[University of Manchester]]. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref>

==Academic career==
After earning his PhD with Victor Petrashov,<ref name="bbcprofile" /> Geim worked as a research scientist at the Institute for Microelectronics Technology (IMT) at RAS, and from 1990 as a post-doctoral fellow at the universities of [[University of Nottingham|Nottingham]] (twice), [[University of Bath|Bath]], and [[University of Copenhagen|Copenhagen]]. He said that while at Nottingham he could spend his time on research rather than "swimming through Soviet treacle",{{citation needed|date=December 2025}} and determined to leave the Soviet Union.<ref name="PhysicsWorld">[https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2058-7058/19/2/15 "A physicist of many talents"]. ''[[Physics World]]''. February 2006. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref>

He obtained his first tenured position in 1994, when he was appointed associate professor at [[Radboud University Nijmegen]], where he worked on [[mesoscopic physics|mesoscopic]] [[superconductivity]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Geim |first1=A. |last2=Dubonos |first2=S. |last3=Palacios |first3=J. |last4=Grigorieva I. V. |first4=I. |author4-link=Irina Grigorieva (academic) |last5=Henini |first5=M. |last6=Schermer |first6=J. |year=2000 |title=Fine Structure in Magnetization of Individual Fluxoid States |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=85 |issue=7 |pages=1528–1531 |arxiv=cond-mat/0001129 |bibcode=2000PhRvL..85.1528G |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.1528 |pmid=10970546 |s2cid=46281431}}</ref> He later gained Dutch citizenship. One of his doctoral students at Nijmegen was [[Konstantin Novoselov]], who went on to become his main research partner. However, Geim has said that he had an unpleasant time during his academic career in the Netherlands.{{Citation needed|date=November 2025}}

He was offered professorships at Nijmegen and [[Eindhoven]], but turned them down as he found the Dutch academic system too hierarchical and full of petty politicking. "This can be pretty unpleasant at times," he says. "It's not like the British system where every staff member is an equal quantity."<ref name="PhysicsWorld" /> On the other hand, Geim writes in his Nobel lecture that "the situation was a bit surreal because outside the university walls I received a warm-hearted welcome from everyone around, including Jan Kees and other academics."<ref name="NobelLecture">Nobel lecture http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2010/geim_lecture.pdf</ref> (Prof. Jan Kees Maan was the research boss of Geim during his time at Radboud University Nijmegen.)

In 2001, he became a professor of physics at the [[University of Manchester]], and was appointed director of the Manchester Centre for Mesoscience and Nanotechnology in 2002. Geim's wife and long-standing co-author, [[Irina Grigorieva (academic)|Irina Grigorieva]], also moved to Manchester as a lecturer in 2001. The same year, they were joined by Novoselov who moved to Manchester from Nijmegen, which awarded him a PhD in 2004. Geim served as [[Langworthy Professor]] between 2007 and 2013, leaving this endowed professorship to Novoselov in 2012.<ref name=CV/> Also, between 2007 and 2010 Geim was an [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council|EPSRC]] Senior Research Fellow before becoming one of [[Royal Society]] Research Professors.<ref name=CV/><ref name="epsrc">{{Cite web |title=Grants awarded to Andre Geim by the EPRSC |url=http://gow.epsrc.ac.uk/NGBOViewPerson.aspx?PersonId=84019 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131213091016/http://gow.epsrc.ac.uk/NGBOViewPerson.aspx?PersonId=84019 |archive-date=13 December 2013}}</ref>

Geim holds many honorary professorships including those from [[Tsinghua University]] (China), [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]] (Russia), and [[Radboud University Nijmegen]] (Netherlands).<ref name="RUM15Feb10">[http://www.ru.nl/english/koppeling_container/2010/nobelprize_geim/vm/discoverer-graphene/ "Discoverer of graphene back at Radboud University as professor"]{{Dead link|date=August 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. [[Radboud University Nijmegen]]. 15 February 2010. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref>

In 2026, Geim commenced his tenure as a [[Chair (professorship)|chair professor]] at the Faculty of Science of the [[University of Hong Kong]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nobel Laureate Professor Sir Andre Geim Joins HKU as Chair Professor |url=https://www.hku.hk/press/news_detail_28952.html |access-date=2026-02-25 |website=[[University of Hong Kong]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Research==
[[File:Graphen.jpg|thumb|Graphene is an [[Chicken wire (chemistry)|atomic-scale honeycomb lattice]] made of [[carbon]] [[atom]]s.]]
Geim's achievements include the discovery of a simple method for isolating single atomic layers of graphite, known as [[graphene]], in collaboration with researchers at the University of Manchester<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 September 2014 |title=The Story of Graphene |url=http://www.graphene.manchester.ac.uk/explore/the-story-of-graphene/ |access-date=9 October 2014 |publisher=The University of Manchester}}</ref> and IMT. The team published their findings in October 2004 in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]''.<ref name="APS">(October 2009). {{Cite web |title=22 October 2004: Discovery of Graphene |url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200910/loader.cfm?csModule=security/getfile&pageid=187967}}&nbsp;{{small|(2.14&nbsp;MB)}}. ''[[APS News]]'' ([[American Physical Society]]) '''18''' (9): 2. See the online version here [http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200910/physicshistory.cfm].</ref><ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/3944651.stm "Radical fabric is one atom thick"]. [[BBC News]]. 22 October 2004. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref><ref name="eff">{{Cite journal |last1=Novoselov |first1=K. S. |author-link=Konstantin Novoselov |last2=Geim |first2=A. K. |author-link2=Andre Geim |last3=Morozov |first3=S. V. |last4=Jiang |first4=D. |last5=Zhang |first5=Y. |last6=Dubonos |first6=S. V. |last7=Grigorieva |first7=I. V. |author7-link=Irina Grigorieva (academic) |last8=Firsov |first8=A. A. |year=2004 |title=Electric Field Effect in Atomically Thin Carbon Films |url=http://www.condmat.physics.manchester.ac.uk/pdf/mesoscopic/publications/graphene/Science_2004.pdf |journal=Science |volume=306 |issue=5696 |pages=666–669 |arxiv=cond-mat/0410550 |bibcode=2004Sci...306..666N |doi=10.1126/science.1102896 |pmid=15499015 |s2cid=5729649}}</ref>

Graphene consists of one-atom-thick layers of [[carbon]] [[atom]]s arranged in two-dimensional hexagons,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sanderson |first=K. |year=2007 |title=Carbon makes super-tough paper |journal=News@nature |doi=10.1038/news070723-7|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>Palmer, Jason. [https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/7827148.stm "Bendy gadget future for graphene"]. [[BBC News]]. 14 January 2009. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref> and is the thinnest material in the world, as well as one of the strongest and hardest.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Overbye |first1=Dennis |author1-link=Dennis Overbye |title=Physics Nobel Honors Work on Ultra-Thin Carbon |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/10/06/science/06nobel.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=March 30, 2023 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 5, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140924123720/http://www.nytimes.com/2010/10/06/science/06nobel.html?pagewanted=all |archive-date=2014-09-24}}{{cbignore}}</ref> The material has many potential applications.

Geim said one of the first applications of graphene could be in the development of flexible [[touchscreen]]s, and that he has not patented the material because he would need a specific application and an industrial partner.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brumfiel |first=G. |year=2010 |title=Andre Geim: In praise of graphene |journal=Nature |doi=10.1038/news.2010.525}}</ref>

Geim also developed a [[Bionics|biomimetic]] adhesive which became known as [[gecko tape]]<ref name="gecko" />—so called because it works on the same principle as adhesion of [[gecko]] feet—research of which is still in the early stages.<ref>Black, Richard. [https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/2953852.stm "Gecko inspires sticky tape"]. [[BBC News]]. 1 June 2003. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref> It is hoped that the development will eventually allow humans to scale ceilings, like [[Spider-Man]].<ref>Highfield, Roger. [https://web.archive.org/web/20090723154344/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/science/science-news/3322870/Gecko-lizards-inspire-Spiderman-gloves.html "Gecko lizards inspire 'Spiderman gloves'"]. ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]''. 23 January 2008. Retrieved 25 October 2010.</ref>

Geim's research in 1997 into the possible effects of magnetism on water scaling led to the famous discovery of direct [[diamagnetic levitation]] of water, and led to a frog being levitated.<ref>[http://www.ru.nl/hfml/research/levitation/diamagnetic/ "The Frog That Learned to Fly"]. [[Radboud University Nijmegen]]. Retrieved 19 October 2010. For Geim's account of diamagnetic levitation, see Geim, Andrey. {{Cite journal |last=Geim |first=Andrey |date=September 1998 |title=Everyone's Magnetism |url=https://www.physics.umd.edu/grt/taj/411c/EveryonesMagnetism.pdf |journal=[[Physics Today]] |volume=51 |pages=36–39 |bibcode=1998PhT....51i..36G |doi=10.1063/1.882437 |doi-access=free |number=9}}</ref> For this experiment, he and [[Michael Berry (physicist)|Michael Berry]] received the 2000 Ig Nobel Prize.<ref name="frog" /> "We were asked first whether we dared to accept this prize, and I take pride in our sense of humor and self-deprecation that we did".<ref name="NobelBio" />

Geim has also carried out research on [[mesoscopic physics]] and [[superconductivity]].<ref name="PhysicsWorld" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Geim |first1=A. K. |last2=Grigorieva |first2=I. V. |author2-link=Irina Grigorieva (academic) |last3=Dubonos |first3=S. V. |last4=Lok |first4=J. G. S. |last5=Maan |first5=J. C. |last6=Filippov |first6=A. E. |last7=Peeters |first7=F. M. |year=1997 |title=Phase transitions in individual sub-micrometre superconductors |journal=Nature |volume=390 |issue=6657 |pages=259 |bibcode=1997Natur.390..259G |doi=10.1038/36797 |s2cid=4418440}}</ref>

He said of the range of subjects he has studied: "Many people choose a subject for their PhD and then continue the same subject until they retire. I despise this approach. I have changed my subject five times before I got my first tenured position and that helped me to learn different subjects."<ref name=Murphy/> "When one dares to try, rewards are not guaranteed but at least it is an adventure."<ref name="NobelBio" />

Expanding the scope of his research adventures, Geim started studying low-dimensional water in 2012, after his Nobel-prize achievements. A part of this work was acknowledged by the 2018 [[Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Prize for Water#The Creativity Prize|Prince Sultan Bin Abdulaziz International Creativity Prize for Water]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Announcement |title=PSIPW |url=https://www.psipw.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=408&Itemid=290&lang=en |access-date=12 July 2018 |website=www.psipw.org |language=en-gb}}</ref>

He named his favourite hamster, H.A.M.S. ter Tisha, co-author in a 2001 research paper.<ref name=APS/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Geim |first1=A. K. |last2=Ter Tisha |first2=H. A. M. S. |year=2001 |title=Detection of earth rotation with a diamagnetically levitating gyroscope |journal=Physica B: Condensed Matter |volume=294–295 |pages=736–739 |bibcode=2001PhyB..294..736G |doi=10.1016/S0921-4526(00)00753-5 |hdl=10498/19331|url=https://repository.ubn.ru.nl//bitstream/handle/2066/249681/249681.pdf |archive-date=2024-04-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240412223905/https://repository.ubn.ru.nl//bitstream/handle/2066/249681/249681.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=2026-10-10}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
In 2006, he appeared on the ''[[Scientific American]]'' 50.<ref>[http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=scientific-american-50-sa-2006-12 "Scientific American 50: SA 50 Winners and Contributors"]. ''[[Scientific American]]''. 12 November 2006. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref> The [[Institute of Physics]] awarded him the 2007 [[Nevill Mott Medal and Prize|Mott Medal and Prize]] "for his discovery of a new class of materials—free-standing two-dimensional crystals—in particular graphene".<ref>[http://www.iop.org/about/awards/subject/mott/medallists/page_45058.html "2007 Mott medal and prize"]. [[Institute of Physics]]. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref> Geim was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2007|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2007]].<ref name="frs">{{Cite web |title=Certificate of Election: EC/2007/16: Andre Geim |url=http://royalsociety.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190704215133/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=%28RefNo%3D%3D%27EC%2F2007%2F16%27%29 |archive-date=4 July 2019 |publisher=The Royal Society |location=London}}</ref> His certificate of election reads: {{centered pull quote|Geim's research is notable for its internationally-recognised quality, originality and breadth. He has recently discovered a conceptually new class of materials strictly two-dimensional atomic crystals, including graphene. This has opened up a prolific research area including a new paradigm of "relativistic-like condensed matter", where relativistic quantum physics can be studied in a bench-top experiment. Previously, Geim pioneered ballistic Hall micromagnetometry and discovered a paramagnetic [[Meissner effect]] and new vortex physics in superconductors. He has also realised a microfabricated adhesive, based on the gecko's climbing mechanism, now being exploited by [[DuPont]], [[BAE Systems|BAe]] and TESA. His experiments at [[Nijmegen]] on magnetic levitation attracted worldwide media attention and stimulated international research in this field. His earlier research on mesoscopic physics included studies of non-local and interaction phenomena, and of the quantum motion of electrons in periodic and random magnetic fields. He disseminates science to the public and schoolchildren through broadcasts and "roadshow" lectures.<ref name=frs/>}}

He shared the 2008 [[EPS Europhysics Prize]] with Novoselov "for discovering and isolating a single free-standing atomic layer of carbon (graphene) and elucidating its remarkable electronic properties".<ref>Johnston, Hamish. [http://physicsworld.com/cws/article/news/35665 "Graphene pioneers bag Europhysics prize"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829145712/http://physicsworld.com/cws/article/news/35665 |date=29 August 2010 }}. ''[[Physics World]]''. 2 September 2008. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref> In 2009 he received the [[Körber European Science Award]].<ref>[http://www.manchester.ac.uk/aboutus/news/display/?id=4582 "Graphene pioneer wins major international prize"]. [[University of Manchester]]. 21 April 2009. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref> The US [[National Academy of Sciences]] honoured him with the 2010 [[John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science]] "for his experimental realisation and investigation of graphene, the two-dimensional form of carbon".<ref>[http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_carty "John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229180532/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_carty |date=29 December 2010 }}. United States [[National Academy of Sciences]]. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref>

He was awarded one of six Royal Society 2010 Anniversary Research Professorships.<ref>[http://royalsociety.org/Top-researchers-receive-Royal-Society-2010-Anniversary-Professorships "Top researchers receive Royal Society 2010 Anniversary Professorships"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101008163856/http://royalsociety.org/Top-researchers-receive-Royal-Society-2010-Anniversary-Professorships/ |date=8 October 2010 }}. [[Royal Society]]. 16 October 2009. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref> The Royal Society added its 2010 [[Hughes Medal]] "for his revolutionary discovery of graphene and elucidation of its remarkable properties".<ref>[http://royalsociety.org/Hughes-Medal/ "The Hughes Medal (1902)"]. [[Royal Society]]. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref> He was awarded honorary doctorates from [[Delft University of Technology]],<ref>[http://www.tudelft.nl/live/pagina.jsp?id=b36143b4-4131-45b2-9c64-e0e8035a6215&lang=en "TU Delft honorary doctorate Geim wins Nobel Prize for graphene research"]{{Dead link|date=August 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. [[Delft University of Technology]]. 5 October 2010. Retrieved 24 October 2010.</ref> [[ETH Zürich]],<ref name=RUM15Feb10/> the [[University of Antwerp]]<ref>[http://www.ua.ac.be/main.aspx?c=CMT&n=37774 "Prizes and awards"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306022833/http://www.ua.ac.be/main.aspx?c=CMT&n=37774 |date=6 March 2012 }}. [[University of Antwerp]]. Retrieved 25 October 2010.</ref> and the [[University of Manchester]]. In 2010, Geim was appointed as [[Order of the Netherlands Lion|Knight Commander of the Order of the Netherlands Lion]] for his contribution to Dutch Science.<ref name="rijksoverheid.nl" /> 

In 2011, Geim became a corresponding member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andre Geim |url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/11673 |access-date=24 January 2016 |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |archive-date=30 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160130194054/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/11673 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is [[Honorary professorship|Honorary Professor]] of Moscow Phys-Tech, Honorary Professor of the University of Nijmegen, [[Honorary Fellow]] of the [[Institute of Physics]] (HonFInstP), [[Honorary Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (HonFRSC), Honorary Fellow of [[Singapore Institute of Physics]], Honorary Professor of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=(IUCr) A. Geim |url=http://www.iucr.org/people/nobel-prize/geim |website=iucr.org}}</ref> Geim was furthermore made a [[Knight Bachelor]] in the [[2012 New Year Honours]] for services to science.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=60009 |date=31 December 2011 |page=1 |supp=y}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=31 December 2011 |title=Knighthoods for Nobel-winning graphene pioneers |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-16362899}}</ref> He was elected a foreign associate of the [[US National Academy of Sciences]] in May 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 May 2012 |title=National Academy of Sciences Members and Foreign Associates Elected |url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2012_05_01_NAS_Election.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120504002407/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2012_05_01_NAS_Election.html |archive-date=4 May 2012 |publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Copley Medal]] in 2013 and the [[Carbon Medal]] in 2016. Geim received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration |website=www.achievement.org |publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]}}</ref> In addition to this he also won the 2018 Fray International Sustainability Award given to him by FLOGEN Star Outreach at SIPS 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andre Geim winner of the Fray Award |url=https://www.flogen.org/?p=38&bio=Geim}}</ref>
===Ig Nobel Prize in Physics===
[[File:Frog diamagnetic levitation.jpg|upright|thumb|Magnetically levitating a live frog, an experiment that earned Geim and [[Michael Berry (physicist)|Michael Berry]] the 2000 [[Ig Nobel Prize]]]]
Geim shared the [[List_of_Ig_Nobel_Prize_winners#2000|2000]] [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in Physics with [[Sir Michael Berry]] for the frog experiment. The experiment involved magnetic properties of water scaling to [[magnetic levitation|levitate]] a small [[frog]] with [[magnets]],<ref>[http://improbable.com/ig/winners/#ig2000 "Winners of the Ig Nobel Prize"]. [[Ig Nobel Prize]]. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref> which he and Berry reported in the ''[[European Journal of Physics]]'' in 1997.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berry |first1=M. V. |last2=Geim |first2=A. K. |date=1997 |title=Of flying frogs and levitrons |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1088/0143-0807/18/4/012 |journal=European Journal of Physics |language=en |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=307 |doi=10.1088/0143-0807/18/4/012 |bibcode=1997EJPh...18..307B |issn=0143-0807 |s2cid=1499061|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

By 2022, his Ig Nobel Prize-winning work on the magnetic levitation of a frog was reportedly part of the inspiration for China's [[Gravitation of the Moon#Simulating lunar gravity|lunar gravity research]] facility.<ref name="Futurism01a">{{Cite web |title=China building "Artificial Moon" that simulates low gravity with magnets |url=https://futurism.com/the-byte/china-artificial-moon-magnets |access-date=17 January 2022 |website=Futurism.com |date=12 January 2022 |publisher=Recurrent Ventures |quote=Interestingly, the facility was partly inspired by previous research conducted by Russian physicist Andrew Geim in which he floated a frog with a magnet. The experiment earned Geim the Ig Nobel Prize in Physics, a satirical award given to unusual scientific research. It’s cool that a quirky experiment involving floating a frog could lead to something approaching an honest-to-God antigravity chamber.}}</ref><ref name="scmp2022-01-12a">{{Cite web |last=Stephen Chen |date=12 January 2022 |title=China has built an artificial moon that simulates low-gravity conditions on Earth |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3162972/china-has-built-artificial-moon-simulates-low-gravity-conditions |access-date=17 January 2022 |publisher=[[South China Morning Post]] |quote=It is said to be the first of its kind and could play a key role in the country’s future lunar missions. Landscape is supported by a magnetic field and was inspired by experiments to levitate a frog.}}</ref>
===Nobel Prize in Physics===
[[File:Nobel Prize 2010-Press Conference KVA-DSC 8019.jpg|250px|thumb|[[Peter Diamond]], [[Dale T. Mortensen]], [[Christopher A. Pissarides]], [[Konstantin Novoselov]], Andre Geim, [[Akira Suzuki (chemist)|Akira Suzuki]], [[Ei-ichi Negishi]], and [[Richard Heck]], Nobel Prize Laureates 2010, at a press conference at the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] in Stockholm.]]
On 5 October 2010, Geim was awarded the 2010 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] jointly with Novoselov "for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene".<ref>[http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2010/ "The Nobel Prize in Physics 2010"]. Nobel Prize. Retrieved 26 October 2010. For a video of the announcement, see [http://nobelprize.org/mediaplayer/index.php?id=1369 "Announcement of the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics"]. Nobel Prize. Retrieved 26 October 2010. For the interview with Geim following the award, see [http://nobelprize.org/mediaplayer/index.php?id=1380 "Telephone interview with Andre Geim"]. Nobel Prize. Retrieved 26 October 2010.</ref> Upon hearing of the award he said, "I'm fine, I slept well. I didn't expect the Nobel Prize this year", and that his plans for the day would not change.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-11476301 "Materials breakthrough wins Nobel"]. [[BBC News]]. 5 October 2010. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref> The lecture for the award took place on 8 December 2010 at [[Stockholm University]].<ref>[http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2010/geim-lecture.html "Nobel Lecture"]. Nobel Prize. Retrieved 26 October 2010.</ref> He said he hopes that graphene and other two-dimensional crystals will change everyday life as plastics did for humanity, although we need to wait for a few decades to see the results.<ref>[http://edition.cnn.com/2010/LIVING/10/05/sweden.nobel.physics/index.html?hpt=T2 "Research into graphene wins Nobel Prize"]. [[CNN]]. 5 October 2010. Retrieved 19 October 2010.</ref>

[[Mark Miodownik]] said that his Ig Nobel Prize shows that people can still win a Nobel by "mucking about in a lab".<ref>Alleyne, Richard. [https://web.archive.org/web/20101007002015/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/science/science-news/8043657/Mucking-about-with-pencil-lead-and-sticky-tape-wins-Nobel-Prize-for-Physics.html "'Mucking about' with pencil lead and sticky tape wins Nobel Prize for Physics"]. ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]''. 5 October 2010. Retrieved 25 October 2010.</ref> The awards made him the first person to win, as an individual, both a Nobel Prize and an Ig Nobel Prize.<ref>{{Cite web |date=5 October 2010 |title=Geim becomes first Nobel & Ig Nobel winner |url=http://improbable.com/2010/10/05/geim-becomes-first-nobel-ig-nobel-winner/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101009020914/http://improbable.com/2010/10/05/geim-becomes-first-nobel-ig-nobel-winner/ |archive-date=9 October 2010 |access-date=19 October 2010 |website=[[Annals of Improbable Research|Improbable Research]]}}</ref> On winning both the prizes, he has stated that

{{quote|text="Frankly, I value both my Ig Nobel prize and Nobel prize at the same level and for me Ig Nobel prize was the manifestation that I can take jokes, a little bit of [[self-deprecation]] always helps."<ref name="bbcprofile" />}}

2010, Geim was inducted into the [[Guinness World Records]] as the "First individual to win both a Nobel and Ig Nobel prize".<ref>{{Cite web |title=First individual to win both a Nobel and Ig Nobel prize |url=https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/first-individual-to-win-both-a-nobel-and-ig-nobel-prize |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=Guinness World Records |language=en-gb}}</ref>

==Personal life==

===View and opinions===
Geim was one of 38 Nobel laureates who signed a declaration in 2010 issued by Scholars for Peace in the Middle East protesting an international initiative to [[Academic boycotts of Israel|boycott]] Israeli academics, institutions, and research centres.<ref>[http://www.spme.net/cgi-bin/articles.cgi?ID=7322 Statement]. Scholars for Peace in the Middle East. 28 October 2010. Retrieved 10 July 2011.</ref>

At the ''Nobel Minds'' symposium in December 2010, Geim said the [[Nobel Peace Prize]] committee's choice of Chinese dissident, the imprisoned [[Liu Xiaobo]], as winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, was patronising, saying 
<blockquote>"Look at the people who give this Nobel prize. They are retired Norwegian politicians who have spent all their careers in a safe environment, in an oil-rich modern country. They try to extend their views of the world, how the world should work and how democracy works in another country. It's very, very patronising— they have not lived in these countries. In the past 10 years, China has developed not only economically, but even the strongest human rights supporter would agree also human rights have improved. Why do we need to distort this?"<ref>[http://nobelprize.org/mediaplayer/index.php?id=1469 "2010 Nobel Minds"]. nobelprize.org. Passage begins at about 19:00. Retrieved 10 July 2011.</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Bannerman |first=Lucy |title=Liu Xiaobo wrong man for Nobel Peace Prize, say laureates |date=13 December 2010 |work=[[The Australian]] |access-date=10 July 2011 |archive-date=2011-01-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110121180001/http://www.theaustralian.com.au/news/world/liu-xiaobo-wrong-man-for-nobel-peace-prize-say-laureates/story-e6frg6so-1225969772275 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/nation/world/liu-xiaobo-wrong-man-for-nobel-peace-prize-say-laureates/news-story/fa9dcb079ecd8c057cd5d12888dc1cf4}}</ref></blockquote>

Geim has written several opinion pieces for ''[[The Financial Times]]'', examples of which can be found on his university webpage.<ref>{{URL|http://www.condmat.physics.manchester.ac.uk/people/academic/geim/}}</ref>

Geim was interviewed in 2014 for ''[[Desert Island Discs]]'', a popular BBC radio programme. His music choices included ''[[Non, je ne regrette rien]]'' by [[Édith Piaf]], and his luxury was [[Amarone]] wine.<ref>{{URL|http://www.bbc.co.uk/radio4/features/desert-island-discs/castaway/20e3bf76#b03z3l2g}}</ref>

A quote from Geim was deliberately doctored by the campaign group [[Vote Leave]] in the run-up to the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum]]. An open letter about science, signed by 13 Conservative MPs including [[Boris Johnson]], attempted to paint European science funding as unnecessarily bureaucratic and deliberately misrepresented Geim's views on Europe:

<blockquote>As the Nobel Prize winner Andre Geim said: 'I can offer no nice words for the EU framework programmes <nowiki>[for research]</nowiki> which ... can be praised only by Europhobes for discrediting the whole idea of an effectively working Europe.'</blockquote>

The [[ellipsis]] (...) present in the quotation from Geim's Nobel lecture removed the words "except for the [[European Research Council]]".<ref>{{Cite web |date=16 October 2019 |title=Dominic Cummings' science obsession: based on fact or fiction? |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/dominic-cummings-science-obsession-based-fact-or-fiction |access-date=25 November 2019 |website=Times Higher Education (THE) |language=en}}</ref>

In 2025, Geim automatically lost his Dutch citizenship due to his dual British nationality.<ref name="citizen" />

===Identity===
Geim has a complex ancestry which is described in detail in his Nobel Prize [[autobiography]].<ref name="NobelBio" /> There, Geim stated that most of his family are [[ethnic Germans]], his father descended from [[Volga German]]s and his mother mostly an [[ethnic German]] as well. Both his father and paternal grandfather had spent many years of their lives as prisoners in [[Siberia]] in [[Stalin]]'s [[Gulags]], and "some of the family had been prisoners in German concentration camps". He also states that he "suffered from [[Antisemitism in the Soviet Union|anti-Semitism in Russia]] because my name sounds Jewish".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weinreb |first=Gali |date=16 November 2010 |title=Nobel Laureate Geim: Life sciences suited for small countries |url=http://www.globes.co.il/serveen/globes/docview.asp?did=1000600865 |access-date=13 December 2019 |publisher=[[Globes (newspaper)|Globes]]}}</ref>

Geim summarises his identity as follows. "To the best of my knowledge, the only Jew in the family was my great-grandmother, with the rest on both sides being German. Having lived and worked in several European countries, I consider myself European and do not believe that any further [[taxonomy (general)|taxonomy]] is necessary, especially in such a fluid world as the world of science."<ref name="NobelBio" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nobel laureate: Life sciences suited to small countries |url=https://www.jpost.com/Business/BusinessNews/Article.aspx?id=196080 |website=The Jerusalem Post - JPost.com}}</ref>
